[ELMALILI:75:31-35/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | A report mentioned earlier says this verse was revealed about Abu Jahl.
[ELMALILI:75:31-35/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Although reported about Abu Jahl, the verse plainly applies to others with the same traits.
[ELMALILI:75:31-35/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Such a man will not be among the laughing faces: he will suffer a dire fate, with his back broken and a dark, distressed face.
[ELMALILI:75:31-35/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The Arabic idiom is a prayer of vindication, like Turkish “this calamity was deserved—serve you right.”
[ELMALILI:75:31-35/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Elmalılı relates awlā laka to awlā as “more fitting for you”: woe and destruction are what befit you.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p363#2/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · قتادة | reports | Qatada reports that the Prophet seized Abu Jahl at the mosque door and threatened him with this wording; Abu Jahl boasted of his strength, and the revelation answered him.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p363#2/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The Prophet used the revealed threat against Abu Jahl as a warning for people like him; early scholars' claims that an event occasioned revelation can be stated loosely.
[TABATABAI:75:31-36/r10] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · قيل | reports | Alternatively, God is the hidden subject and the lām is extra (‘God gives you what you hate’) or original (‘God brings you near what you hate’).
[TABATABAI:75:31-36/r11] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · قيل | reports | Another gloss supplies an omitted word: blame is more fitting than leaving it unsaid; the phrase became like ‘woe to you.’
[TABATABAI:75:31-36/r12] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · قيل | reports | A further gloss is ‘May God destroy you with a destruction nearer than every other evil and ruin.’
[TABATABAI:75:31-36/r13] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · قيل | reports | Another analysis takes awla as a comparative adjective with an omitted predicate: Hell is most fitting for you, or you deserve it.
[TABATABAI:75:31-36/r14] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | rejects | The reported explanations are weak or strained; the last is close to the author’s reading but does not fully match it.
[TABATABAI:75:31-36/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The repeated threat intensifies the warning; ‘better for you’ predicates an omitted subject referring to his conduct, metonymically assigning its burden and punishment.

[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p82/r1] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The disbelievers face an exacting journey without provisions: they neither prayed nor spent in God’s way, the two deeds that would benefit them.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p84/r3] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | Wayl expresses anger, reproach, and hatred and is common in classical Arabic; Khansā’s verse illustrates this reproach, while translating it as “befitting” violates Arabic usage and context.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p84/r4] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The shift from indirect speech to direct address conveys sorrow and hatred.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p227/r3] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | Awlā laka is a warning and threat meaning ‘woe to you’; from w-l-y, nearness, its comparative form suggests destruction is close.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p227/r4] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · الكشاف | reports | Al-Kashshāf glosses the related awlā lahum as a threat meaning woe, from nearness, a prayer that misfortune come close to them.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p227/r5] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · روح المعاني | reports | Rūḥ al-Maʿānī explains the phrase as a comparative originally, used for approaching ruin and a prayer for evil to be near.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p227/r6] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Aṣmaʿī's usage in al-Ṣiḥāḥ takes the expression to mean that what destroys someone has drawn near.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p227/r7] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · قيل | reports | Another reported view treats awlā as a fixed verbal expression meaning one evil follows another.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p228/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | The urgent threat fits people who chose immediate pleasures and sins and delayed obedience: just as they hurried into sin, ruin is hurried toward them, within the sūra's theme of haste.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p228/r2] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | Unlike Muhammad's single warning, this passage repeats awlā inside the verse and repeats the whole verse, repeats awlā but not laka, separates the inner warnings with fa, and separates the verses with thumma. | mentions 47:20
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p228/r3] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | The different wording follows different contexts: Muhammad depicts hesitant people facing the prospect of fighting, while Qiyāma describes a denier who rejects faith and prayer and walks off arrogantly. | mentions 47:20, 75:31, 75:32, 75:33
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p229/r4] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | The Muhammad group are described while alive, when repentance remains possible; the Qiyāma person is described after death, having died in denial and facing the realized threat. | mentions 47:20
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p229/r5] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | Muhammad names one trait, cowardice before fighting, so the threat occurs once; Qiyāma names multiple forms of disbelief, warranting repeated threats. | mentions 47:20
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p230/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | Each of the two faults first receives a warning; the second verse restates them as denial and turning away, so the author counts four warnings, one for each fault in both formulations.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p231/r2] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | The stronger ‘awlā laka’ answers unbelief, while the threat for not praying omits laka; the difference marks the gravity of faith, though the verse ending also supports the omission.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p232/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · author | holds | Thumma can mark distance in rank, not only time: the Qur'anic example in 90:11–17 distinguishes freeing and feeding from faith, so the later threat is more forceful. | mentions 90:11, 90:12, 90:13, 90:14, 90:15, 90:16, 90:17
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p232/r2] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT · قيل | reports | A reported view says the repetition intensifies the warning and threat.
